title: L2 (CRUX): super-polynomial upper bound on sigma_i(A)

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
**This is the crux of the problem.** Prove a super-polynomial UPPER bound on $\sigma_i(A)$, i.e. that for every $\kappa>0$, $\sigma_i(A)=o(i^{-\kappa})$. Equivalently, prove an explicit decay bound such as $\sigma_i(A)\le C\,\rho^{-i}$ for some $\rho>1$ (plain exponential already answers the dichotomy), ideally strengthened to the observed super-exponential rate.

**Why the naive bound fails.** Submultiplicativity gives only $\sigma_i(A)\le\|B^{(H)}\|\,\sigma_i(J)=\sqrt{\pi}\,/((i-\tfrac12)\pi)\asymp i^{-1}$, which is a degree-1 *moderate* upper bound and does NOT exclude moderate ill-posedness. One cannot factor singular values of a product; the amplification by the non-compact moment operator must be analyzed directly via the kernel $(\star)$.

**Suggested routes.**
1. *Analytic n-width / Chebyshev-truncation route.* The functions $A^*e_i=(1-t^i)/i$ are boundary values of functions analytic in a neighbourhood of $[0,1]$ in $\mathbb C$. Use $\sigma_{n+1}(A)=\min_{\mathrm{rank}\,T\le n}\|A-T\|$ and build an explicit rank-$n$ approximant from a degree-$n$ polynomial/Chebyshev truncation of the kernel $k(s,t)=\sum_i e_i\otimes J^*(s^{i-1})$; analyticity gives remainder $\le C\rho^{-n}$. Cite Pinkus, *n-Widths in Approximation Theory* (exponential width decay for analyticity classes).
2. *Hilbert/Hankel-matrix asymptotics.* Write $(\star)=D\,\mathcal M\,D$, $D=\mathrm{diag}(1/i)$, with $\mathcal M$ a low-rank perturbation of Hilbert-type entries $1/(i+j+1)$; apply Widom's Hankel-determinant asymptotics / Szegő strong limit theorem to extract the rate.

**Numerical target (80–120 digit mpmath, truncated $(\star)$):** $\sigma_1,\dots\approx 0.858,0.140,0.0362,0.0112,0.00369,\dots$, consecutive ratios $\sigma_i/\sigma_{i+1}\approx 3.0,3.0,3.0,3.1,3.2,\dots,5.3$ *increasing roughly linearly in $i$* (second differences $\approx +0.08$), i.e. faster than any geometric decay.

**Difficulty:** high. This is the load-bearing estimate; it requires genuine spectral/approximation-theoretic input, not a routine bound.
